idiom_name: tag types + trait mapping + ordered overload ladder + single public entry point
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one empty tag type per decision outcome and relate them to one another (inheritance, ordering, or constraint subsumption) so that a more specific tag is also a valid less specific one; map each client type to its tag through a trait, instance or marker type (never by editing the client type); write one implementation per tag in a detail namespace; expose exactly one public function that derives the tag from the caller's type and forwards to the ladder. The tag is a compile-time artefact: it is never read, stored or compared, and the whole mechanism must disappear after optimization. Provide an unconstrained fallback level, and turn the 'no implementation for this type' case into a single clear compile-time diagnostic.
code_sketch:
tag_for<T>::type                     # maps a client type to its tag (trait/instance)
impl(x, TagA{}) { ... }              # one complete implementation per tag
impl(x, TagB{}) { ... }              #   related by inheritance -> priority + fallback
public f(x) { impl(x, tag_for<T>::type{}); }   # tag never escapes, never read
pitfalls: Letting the tag escape into the public API or into stored state: it then becomes data, and the runtime cost the pattern avoids comes back.
Omitting the fallback level, or constraining it, so that a type without an exact match fails with an error that names the ladder instead of the type.
Assuming the ladder is exhaustive: a missing level silently promotes the tag to a less specific one.

Wrong move: testing tag identity with exact equality (std::is_same, == on an enum tag); failure: a richer tag that derives from the tested one fails the check and the optimized path is silently skipped - LLVM replaced is_same with is_base_of for random_access_iterator_tag checks for exactly this reason; instead: ask the subtyping question (is_base_of, constraint subsumption, convertible-to) so the ladder's own ranking is what you test.

Wrong move: building the tag from a value only known at run time (Val(n), a tag made from configuration); failure: selection degrades to a runtime lookup that still pays every instantiation - Julia's own docs warn that dispatch on a non-constant Val is slower than a plain branch; instead: feed tags from literals and type parameters only, and use a normal branch when the value is dynamic.

Wrong move: inserting a new, more specific tag level without auditing existing resolutions; failure: call sites that previously selected the fallback silently rebind to the new level, changing behaviour for types the new overload was never written for, with no diagnostic; instead: pin each level's intended selection with static_asserts or tests on the chosen overload before the new level lands.
